title: Recreating Disease to Test Its Cause
endLine: Animal models recreate disease features to test cause, not copy people.

scenes.tts: How do you test what causes a disease, without experimenting on patients? Watching patients shows what fails, not which broken part came first. To test cause directly, scientists recreate one disease feature inside an animal.
scenes.caption: How do you test what causes a disease, without experimenting on patients? Watching patients shows what fails, not which broken part came first. To test cause directly, scientists recreate one disease feature inside an animal.
scenes.visual: Full-frame dark studio comparator filling most of the frame height (schematic): a human silhouette on the left shows a pulsing symptom alert over a tangled circuit behind a soft barrier labelled "Cannot test here". As the opening question finishes, a glowing bridge opens to an animal silhouette on the right with one highlighted circuit node.
scenes.narration: How do you test what causes a disease, without experimenting on patients? Watching patients shows what fails, not which broken part came first. To test cause directly, scientists recreate one disease feature inside an animal.

scenes.visual: The human-to-animal bridge settles with slow ambient circuit pulses; the title "Recreating Disease to Test Its Cause" fades in clearly at center, then clears while the animal silhouette remains anchored on the right.

scenes.tts: They build that feature with genes, toxins, injury, or patient antibodies. Deleting the muscle protein musk stops nerve-to-muscle junctions from forming in newborn mice. Toxins kill specific brain neurons, and loud noise injures inner ear synapses.
scenes.caption: They build that feature with genes, toxins, injury, or patient antibodies. Deleting the muscle protein MuSK stops nerve-to-muscle junctions from forming in newborn mice. Toxins kill specific brain neurons, and loud noise injures inner ear synapses.
scenes.visual: Zooming onto the right-hand animal silhouette (schematic), four input icons ("Genes", "Toxins", "Injury", "Antibodies") feed sequentially into the same animal: removing a MuSK tag breaks a schematic nerve-to-muscle contact, a toxin drop dims a brain neuron cluster, and sound waves dim inner ear synapses.
scenes.narration: They build that feature with genes, toxins, injury, or patient antibodies. Deleting the muscle protein MuSK stops nerve-to-muscle junctions from forming in newborn mice. Toxins kill specific brain neurons, and loud noise injures inner ear synapses.

scenes.tts: Inside a living animal, researchers can intervene, not only watch. Removing one link at a time in mouse muscle reveals each protein's job. An animal model recreates one disease feature to test cause, never a whole human.
scenes.caption: Inside a living animal, researchers can intervene, not only watch. Removing one link at a time in mouse muscle reveals each protein's job. An animal model recreates one disease feature to test cause, never a whole human.
scenes.visual: Inside the same animal silhouette (schematic), a chain of muscle junction links lights up; an intervention switch toggles one link off at a time and shows the junction output changing. The view pulls back slightly to highlight the single glowing feature ring inside the animal while the human silhouette stays distinct on the left.
scenes.narration: Inside a living animal, researchers can intervene, not only watch. Removing one link at a time in mouse muscle reveals each protein's job. An animal model recreates one disease feature to test cause, never a whole human.

scenes.tts: Now picture a mouse born without one synapse protein. Its gene is meck P two, the mouse version of the gene mutated in Rett syndrome. By young adulthood it has symptoms, yet two histories fit. Either the circuit was built wrong early, or it simply cannot run. Switching that gene on or off late, which two tests separate them?
scenes.caption: Now picture a mouse born without one synapse protein. Its gene is Mecp2, the mouse version of the gene mutated in Rett syndrome. By young adulthood it has symptoms, yet two histories fit. Either the circuit was built wrong early, or it simply cannot run. Switching that gene on or off late, which two tests separate them?
scenes.visual: The animal silhouette shifts into a schematic brain circuit along a birth-to-adulthood timeline (schematic). A dark "Mecp2" tag sits over the circuit as adult symptoms pulse; two branching paths appear above it ("Built wrong early" and "Built fine, cannot run") beside an age-controlled gene switch and the on-screen question.
scenes.narration: Now picture a mouse born without one synapse protein. Its gene is Mecp2, the mouse version of the gene mutated in Rett syndrome. By young adulthood it has symptoms, yet two histories fit. Either the circuit was built wrong early, or it simply cannot run. Switching that gene on or off late, which two tests separate them?

scenes.visual: Hold the schematic brain circuit, the age switch, and both branching paths with slow ambient motion; keep the question "Which two late tests separate them?" crisp and readable at the top while the viewer thinks.

scenes.tts: First, put the gene back after symptoms begin, and watch. Second, take it from a typical mouse after its circuit is built. If symptoms fade on return and appear on late loss, the protein runs the circuit.
scenes.caption: First, put the gene back after symptoms begin, and watch. Second, take it from a typical mouse after its circuit is built. If symptoms fade on return and appear on late loss, the protein runs the circuit.
scenes.visual: In the same schematic circuit, the age switch flips ON after adult symptoms start and the irregular circuit pulse smooths out. Beside it, on a paired typical mouse after its circuit is built, the switch flips OFF and irregular pulses appear, lighting up the "Built fine, cannot run" path.
scenes.narration: First, put the gene back after symptoms begin, and watch. Second, take it from a typical mouse after its circuit is built. If symptoms fade on return and appear on late loss, the protein runs the circuit.

scenes.tts: Clean tests need sharp controls. A knockout deletes a whole protein, removing every job. A knock-in edits one site, keeping the protein to test one role. Measurements can mislead too: after loud noise, a mouse can pass its hearing test. Yet it can lose about half the ribbon synapses at one inner ear spot.
scenes.caption: Clean tests need sharp controls. A knockout deletes a whole protein, removing every job. A knock-in edits one site, keeping the protein to test one role. Measurements can mislead too: after loud noise, a mouse can pass its hearing test. Yet it can lose about half the ribbon synapses at one inner ear spot.
scenes.visual: On the animal side (schematic), a protein block disappears completely ("Knockout"), dimming multiple outputs, then returns with a single glowing edit ("Knock-in") that tests one output. Below it, a schematic hearing-test gauge stays green ("Pass") while about half the inner ear ribbon synapse dots at one spot fade away.

scenes.tts: Even clean mouse results face species limits. One mouse strain, sex, age, and exposure cannot show what holds in people. The antibody cetuximab shrank mouse lung tumours driven by a mutant receptor. Yet in patients, adding it to the drug afatinib as a first treatment did not help.
scenes.caption: Even clean mouse results face species limits. One mouse strain, sex, age, and exposure cannot show what holds in people. The antibody cetuximab shrank mouse lung tumours driven by a mutant receptor. Yet in patients, adding it to the drug afatinib as a first treatment did not help.
scenes.visual: Pulling back to the Human-and-Animal comparator (schematic), a caution barrier lights up across the bridge ("Check in people"). On the animal side a schematic mouse lung tumour shrinks under "Cetuximab", while on the human side the paired tumour readout for "Cetuximab + afatinib" shows no added improvement.
scenes.narration: Even clean mouse results face species limits. One mouse strain, sex, age, and exposure cannot show what holds in people. The antibody cetuximab shrank mouse lung tumours driven by a mutant receptor. Yet in patients, adding it to the drug afatinib as a first treatment did not help.

scenes.tts: Within those limits, animal models unlocked major causes and targets. In 1975, Toyka and colleagues transferred antibodies from patients with muscle-weakening myasthenia gravis into mice. The mice lost muscle junction receptors and had smaller unit signals, called miniatures.
scenes.caption: Within those limits, animal models unlocked major causes and targets. In 1975, Toyka and colleagues transferred antibodies from patients with muscle-weakening myasthenia gravis into mice. The mice lost muscle junction receptors and had smaller unit signals, called miniatures.
scenes.visual: Across the Human-to-Animal bridge (schematic), a milestone tag "1975 · Toyka & colleagues" appears as patient antibodies cross into the mouse; schematic muscle junction receptors thin out and the unit synaptic pulse shrinks.
scenes.narration: Within those limits, animal models unlocked major causes and targets. In 1975, Toyka and colleagues transferred antibodies from patients with muscle-weakening myasthenia gravis into mice. The mice lost muscle junction receptors and had smaller unit signals, called miniatures.

scenes.tts: In 1990, Bergman, Wichmann, and DeLong tested a brain-circuit prediction in monkeys. They used the toxin M P T P to kill dopamine neurons and model Parkinson's disease. A lesion in the S T N, a deep neuron cluster, eased opposite-side signs. That result made the S T N a surgical target.
scenes.caption: In 1990, Bergman, Wichmann, and DeLong tested a brain-circuit prediction in monkeys. They used the toxin MPTP to kill dopamine neurons and model Parkinson's disease. A lesion in the STN, a deep neuron cluster, eased opposite-side signs. That result made the STN a surgical target.
scenes.visual: A milestone tag "1990 · Bergman, Wichmann & DeLong" lights up on a schematic monkey brain-and-body circuit: "MPTP" dims dopamine neurons, then a lesion marker on the left "STN" cluster smooths slowed movement arrows on the opposite side of the body and highlights "STN" as a surgical target.
scenes.narration: In 1990, Bergman, Wichmann, and DeLong tested a brain-circuit prediction in monkeys. They used the toxin MPTP to kill dopamine neurons and model Parkinson's disease. A lesion in the STN, a deep neuron cluster, eased opposite-side signs. That result made the STN a surgical target.

scenes.tts: In 2017, Michalski and colleagues used a knock-in mouse to test the inner ear protein otoferlin. Changing one calcium-binding domain kept the protein present yet lowered the calcium sensitivity of release. Each model isolated one mechanism; human studies confirm what holds in patients.
scenes.caption: In 2017, Michalski and colleagues used a knock-in mouse to test the inner ear protein otoferlin. Changing one calcium-binding domain kept the protein present yet lowered the calcium sensitivity of release. Each model isolated one mechanism; human studies confirm what holds in patients.
scenes.visual: A milestone tag "2017 · Michalski & colleagues" lights up on a schematic inner hair cell: the otoferlin protein remains in place with one glowing edited calcium-binding domain, while calcium-triggered release pulses drop. The view widens back to the Human-and-Animal comparator, pulsing softly across the bridge before fading to the end card.
